items.prose: A pair's formation sd is 0.015. On day 3 of trading the spread p_i − p_j is −0.032.
items.question: What does the desk do?

options.text: Buy i and sell j: i is the cheaper leg and the gap is beyond 0.030

options.why: j is the dearer leg here. Buying it bets on divergence.

options.text: Nothing: the gap is inside 2 sd

feedback.correct: Correct. Long the cheaper leg, i.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare with 0.030 and buy the cheaper leg.

explain.text: |−0.032| > 0.030, so the pair opens. A negative spread means i is cheaper, so buy i and sell j.

items.prose: On the opening day the long leg's normalised price is 1.25.
items.question: How many units does £1 buy?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide £1 by the price.

byKey.price: That is the price, not the units.

items.prose: A round trip: long leg from 1.10 to 1.05, short leg from 1.20 to 1.08, £1 each.
items.question: What is the payoff?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Long leg's return minus short leg's return.

byKey.sign: You flipped the sign: the short leg fell, which is a gain.
byKey.add: You added the short leg's return. A short gains when its price falls.

explain.text: The long leg lost 0.0455 and the short leg gained 0.1000 as its price fell. The payoff is 0.0545.

items.prose: A backtest closes each pair when its spread returns inside 2 sd.
items.question: What does it do to the result, compared with the paper's rule?

options.text: It books only part of each convergence, so it usually earns less and trades more
It earns more by locking in gains early
Nothing, since the trades are the same
options.why: The exits differ, so the trades differ.

feedback.correct: Correct. The paper waits for the crossing.

explain.text: Exiting at the band takes only the first part of each move back to zero. The first-cycle top 20 fall from 14.24% to 11.27%.

items.prose: A cycle's 20 pairs pay £0.90 in all.
items.question: What is the monthly committed figure, by our convention?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide by 20 pairs, then by 6.

items.prose: Our 127 monthly figures give a naive t of 13.55 and a Newey-West t of 8.09.
items.question: Which should the write-up quote?

options.text: The naive t, as the larger is more convincing
options.why: Larger is not more correct; overlap inflates it.

options.text: Neither, as t statistics do not apply to returns
options.why: They apply; they need the overlap correction.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Allow for the overlap.

explain.text: Neighbouring cycles share five of six months, so the naive t overstates the evidence. 8.09 is still large.

items.prose: A pair earns 3.6% gross per cycle from 1.5 round trips.
items.question: What is the break-even cost per trade?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Four trades per round trip.

byKey.trip: You divided by the trips only.

items.prose: Top 20, same day: 1.00% a month on closes and 0.82% on mids.
items.question: How many points a month is the bounce?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the mid figure from the close figure.

byKey.rel: That is the bounce as a share of the close figure.

explain.text: 1.00 − 0.82 = 0.19 points a month come from closes sitting at the bid or the ask.

items.prose: A first run gives 13% a year against the paper's "up to 11%".
items.question: What is the right next step?

options.text: Check the code, list the known gap sources, and report the gap
Try other thresholds until the result is near 11%
options.why: Tuning to the target makes the match meaningless.

feedback.correct: Correct. Explain gaps; do not tune them away.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A replication explains its gaps.

explain.text: Fixed rules, honest gaps. Tuning to the paper's figure guarantees a match that proves nothing.
